title: Measurement of Length and Motion
intro: How long is your pencil? How fast does a bus move? This chapter teaches you how to measure length accurately, what motion means, and how to describe different ways things move.

sections.heading: Why We Need Standard Units
bullets: Long ago, people measured length using body parts — handspan, footstep, cubit (elbow to fingertip).
These differ from person to person, so the same room could measure as different lengths.
Standard units let everyone get the same answer; the metre is the standard unit of length worldwide.
Smaller lengths use millimetre (mm) and centimetre (cm); longer lengths use kilometre (km).

sections.heading: Measuring Length Correctly
bullets: Use a 15-cm or 30-cm scale for short objects, a measuring tape for longer ones.
Place the zero mark of the scale exactly at one end of the object.
Look at the scale straight from above — not from a slant — to avoid an error called parallax.
If the zero edge of the scale is broken, start from another full mark like 1 cm and subtract at the end.
Record the unit along with the number — '12 cm', not just '12'.

sections.heading: Measuring Curved Lengths
bullets: A straight scale cannot measure a curved line directly.
You can lay a thread along the curve, mark the start and end, and then straighten the thread on a scale.
A flexible measuring tape works well around curved shapes like a person's waist or a tree trunk.
Always remember: it's the line you are measuring, so follow it carefully without stretching the thread.

sections.heading: What Is Motion?
bullets: An object is in motion if its position changes with respect to its surroundings as time passes.
An object at rest stays in the same position over time.
A car moving on the road is in motion; a parked car is at rest.
Motion always needs to be judged compared to something that is treated as fixed (a tree, a wall, a milestone).

sections.heading: Types of Motion
bullets: Straight-line (rectilinear) motion: an object moves along a straight path — a marching parade, a car on a straight road.
Circular motion: an object moves along a circular path — the hands of a clock, a stone tied to a string and whirled around.
Periodic motion: an object repeats the same motion in equal time intervals — a swing, a pendulum.
Oscillatory motion is a kind of periodic motion that goes back and forth around a fixed point — a swinging pendulum, a vibrating ruler.
Some objects show more than one type of motion at once — wheels of a moving cycle have circular motion, while the cycle as a whole moves in a straight line.

sections.heading: Distance and How Things Move
bullets: Distance is the total length covered while moving from one place to another.
Two friends starting from the same place can cover different distances if they take different paths.
We measure distance in the same units as length — metres or kilometres.
On a map, scale tells us how a small length on paper stands for a large distance on the ground.

key_takeaways: Standard units like the metre give everyone the same answer when measuring length.
When measuring, place the scale carefully, read at eye level, and always note the unit.
An object is in motion if its position changes with time; otherwise it is at rest.
Motions can be straight-line, circular, or periodic, and an object can have more than one at once.
A thread plus a scale can measure a curved length that a straight scale can't reach.
